questions.content:
Question A.3

| Answer | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| The galaxy moving away speed $V_i$, in part A.2, is only one component of the three component of the galaxy velocity. Thus the average square speed of each galaxy with respect to the center of the cluster is

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_{ri}^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(V_{xi}-V_{xc})^2+(V_{yi}-V_{yc})^2+(V_{zi}-V_{zc})^2\right]$$

Due to isotropic assumption

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_{ri}^2 = \frac{3}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(V_{xi}-V_{xc})^2$$ | 0.5 pts |
| And thus the root mean square of the galaxy speed with respect to the cluster center is

$$V_{rms}^2 = \frac{3}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_{ri}^2 = \frac{3}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_{xi}^2 - 2V_{xc}\frac{3}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_{xi} + 3V_{xc}^2 = \frac{3}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} V_{xi}^2 - 3V_{xc}^2$$

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{f_i-f_0}{f_0}\right)^2 = \frac{c^2}{3}V_{rms}^2$$

$$\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{f_i-f_0}{f_0}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{f_i^2-2f_if_0+f_0^2}{f_0^2}\right) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{f_i^2}{f_0^2} - \frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{f_i}{f_0} + 1$$

$$V_{rms}^2 = \frac{c^2}{3}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{f_i^2}{f_0^2} - \frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{f_i}{f_0} + 1\right)$$

Alternative without approximation: | 0.7 pts |
| The mean kinetic energy of the galaxies with respect to the center of the cluster is

$$\frac{m}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(v_i-V_c)^2 = \frac{m}{2}V_{rms}^2 = \frac{N}{2}kT_{ave}$$

| 0.3 pts |
| Total | 1.5 pts |
questions.answer: > 星系相对星系团中心的方均根速率为 $V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{c^2}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{N}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}\dfrac{f_i^2}{f_0^2} - \dfrac{2}{N}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}\dfrac{f_i}{f_0} + 1\right)$，星系相对星系团中心的平均动能为 $\dfrac{m}{2}V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{N}{2}kT_{ave}$。

questions.title: 第 04 题
tags: 力学/万有引力/引力势能/位力定理
questions.content:
The time average of $d\Gamma/dt$ vanishes.

Now

$$\frac{d\Gamma}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\sum_i \vec{r}_i \cdot \vec{p}_i = \sum_i \frac{d\vec{r}_i}{dt}\cdot \vec{p}_i + \sum_i \vec{r}_i \cdot \frac{d\vec{p}_i}{dt} = \sum_i \vec{v}_i \cdot \vec{p}_i + \sum_i \vec{r}_i \cdot \vec{F}_i = 2K + \sum_i \vec{r}_i \cdot \vec{F}_i$$

where $K$ is the total kinetic energy of the system. Since the gravitational force on the $i$-th particle comes from its interaction with other particles, then

$$\sum_i \vec{r}_i \cdot \vec{F}_i = \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} \vec{r}_i \cdot \vec{F}_{ji} = \sum_{i<j} \vec{F}_{ji}\cdot(\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j) = -\sum_{i<j} G\frac{m_i m_j}{\|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j\|^2}\cdot\frac{(\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j)}{\|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j\|}\cdot(\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j) = -\sum_{i<j} G\frac{m_i m_j}{\|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j\|} = U_{tot}$$

Alternative proof:

$$\sum_{i,j\neq i} \vec{r}_i \cdot \vec{F}_{ji} = \vec{F}_{21}\cdot\vec{r}_1 + \vec{F}_{31}\cdot\vec{r}_1 + \vec{F}_{41}\cdot\vec{r}_1 + \cdots + \vec{F}_{N1}\cdot\vec{r}_1 + \vec{F}_{12}\cdot\vec{r}_2 + \vec{F}_{32}\cdot\vec{r}_2 + \vec{F}_{42}\cdot\vec{r}_2 + \cdots + \vec{F}_{N2}\cdot\vec{r}_2 + \cdots$$

$$= \vec{F}_{12}\cdot(\vec{r}_2 - \vec{r}_1) + \vec{F}_{13}\cdot(\vec{r}_3 - \vec{r}_1) + \vec{F}_{14}\cdot(\vec{r}_4 - \vec{r}_1) + \cdots + \vec{F}_{23}\cdot(\vec{r}_3 - \vec{r}_2) + \vec{F}_{24}\cdot(\vec{r}_4 - \vec{r}_2) + \cdots + \vec{F}_{34}\cdot(\vec{r}_4 - \vec{r}_3) + \cdots = \sum_{i<j} \vec{F}_{ji}\cdot(\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j)$$

$$= -\sum_{i<j} G\frac{m_i m_j}{\|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j\|^2}\cdot\frac{(\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j)}{\|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j\|}\cdot(\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j) = -\sum_{i<j} G\frac{m_i m_j}{\|\vec{r}_i - \vec{r}_j\|} = U_{tot}$$

Thus we have

$$\frac{d\Gamma}{dt} = U + 2K$$

And by taking its time average we obtain

$$\left\langle \frac{d\Gamma}{dt} \right\rangle_t = \langle U + 2K \rangle_t = 0$$

and thus

$$\langle K \rangle_t = -\frac{1}{2}\langle U \rangle_t$$

Therefore $\gamma = \frac{1}{2}$.

| Using Virial theorem, and since the dark matter has the same root mean square speed as the galaxy, then we have $\langle K \rangle = -\frac{1}{2}\langle U \rangle$, $\frac{1}{2}M v_{rms}^2 = \frac{3}{5}\frac{GM^2}{R}$ | 0.3 pts |

Question B.1

| Answer | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Answer B.1: The gravitational attraction for a particle at a distance r from the center of the sphere comes only from particles inside a spherical volume of radius r. For particle inside the sphere with mass $m_s$, assuming the particle is orbiting the center of mass in a circular orbit, we have $\frac{m'(r)m_s}{r^2}=\frac{m_s v_0^2}{r}$ | 0.3 pts |
| with $m'(r)$ is the total mass inside a sphere of radius r, $m'(r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 m_s n$. Thus we have $v(r)=\left(\frac{4\pi G n m_s}{3}\right)^{1/2}r$ | 0.2 pts |
| While for particle outside the sphere, we have $v(r)=\left(\frac{4\pi G n m_s R^3}{3r}\right)^{1/2}$ | 0.2 pts |

![](data/images/2017-ipho-a203c914/2017-IPhO-理论-第一题-答案-1.jpg)
questions.answer:
> 球内：$v(r)=\left(\dfrac{4\pi G n m_s}{3}\right)^{1/2}r$
>
> 球外：$v(r)=\left(\dfrac{4\pi G n m_s R^3}{3r}\right)^{1/2}$

questions.content:
Question B.3

| Answer | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Base on the previous answer in B.1, if the mass of the galaxy comes only from the visible stars, then the galaxy rotation curve should fall proportional to $1/\sqrt{r}$ on the outside at a distance $r > R_g$. But in the figure of problem b) the curve remain constant after $r > R_g$, we can infer from $G\frac{m'(r)m_s}{r^2} = \frac{m_s v_0^2}{r}$ to make $v(r)$ constant, then $m'(r)$ should be proportional to $r$ for $r > R_g$, i.e. for $r > R_g$, $m'(r) = Ar$ with $A$ is a constant. | 0.3 pts |
| While for $r < R_g$, to obtain a linear plot proportional to $r$, then $m'(r)$ should be proportional to $r^3$, i.e. $m'(r) = Br^3$ | 0.3 pts |
| Thus for $r < R_g$ we have $m'(r)=\int_0^r \rho_t(r)4\pi r^2 dr = Br^3$, $dm'(r)=\rho_t(r)4\pi r^2 dr = 3Br^2 dr$, $\rho_t(r)=\frac{3B}{4\pi}$. Thus total mass density | 0.2 pts |
| $m_R=\int_0^{R_g}\frac{3B}{4\pi}4\pi r^2 dr = BR_g^3$ or $B=\frac{m_R}{R_g^3}=\frac{v_0^2}{GR_g^2}$, $\rho(r)=\frac{3v_0^2}{4\pi G R_g^2}-nm_s$. Thus the dark matter mass density | 0.2 pts |

While for $r > R_g$ we have

$$
m'(r) = \int_0^{R_g} \rho(r') 4\pi r'^2 dr' + \int_{R_g}^r \rho(r') 4\pi r'^2 dr' = Ar
$$

$$
m'(r) = m_R + \int_{R_g}^r \rho(r') 4\pi r'^2 dr' = Ar \tag{0.2 pts}
$$

$$
\int_R^r \rho(r') 4\pi r'^2 dr' = Ar - M_0
$$

$$
\rho(r) 4\pi r^2 = A, \text{ or } \rho(r) = \frac{A}{4\pi r^2}.
$$

Now to find the constant A.

$$
\int_R^r \frac{A}{4\pi r'^2} 4\pi r'^2 dr = A(r - R_g) = Ar - m_R
$$

Thus $AR_g = m_R$ and $A = \frac{v_0^2}{G}$

We can also find A from the following

$$
G\frac{m'(r)m_s}{r^2} = G\frac{Arm_s}{r^2} = \frac{m_s v_0^2}{r}, \text{ thus } A = \frac{v_0^2}{G}. \tag{0.3 pts}
$$

Thus the dark matter mass density (which is also the total mass density since $n \approx 0$ for $r \geq R_g$)

$$
\rho(r) = \frac{v_0^2}{4\pi G r^2} \text{ for } r \geq R_g
$$

C. Interstellar Gas and Dark Matter
